To interpret the EU's treaty and rule in court cases about EU rules.
How many members does the European Parliament have, and how many are elected in Denmark?
720 members, 15 of them from Denmark.
How often does the presidency of the Council of Ministers change, and when did Denmark last hold it?
Every six months. The last Danish EU presidency was in 2025.
What is the Council of Europe?
An independent organisation of 47 European countries. Denmark has been a member since 1949.
What is the European Convention on Human Rights?
Adopted by the Council of Europe – contains fundamental rights such as freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, the ban on torture and the right to a fair trial.
When was the UN founded, and how many members does it have?
1945 – 193 states. Denmark has been a member from the start.
What is the purpose of the UN?
To create peace and development in the world, help in disasters and promote human rights.
Which countries have a permanent seat on the UN Security Council?
France, China, Russia, the UK and the USA. The other ten members are elected for two years at a time.
When is Denmark a member of the UN Security Council?
What can the UN Security Council do against a country that attacks others or oppresses population groups?
Impose economic or military sanctions – and use military force if the country is seen as a threat to international security.
How many Global Goals does the UN have, and when were they adopted?
17 Sustainable Development Goals – adopted in September 2015 in New York. They apply to all countries.
Which countries and territories make up the Nordic region (Norden)?
Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Iceland plus the Faroe Islands, Greenland and the Åland Islands.
What are the Nordic cooperation bodies called?
The Nordic Council and the Nordic Council of Ministers.
How large is Denmark's development aid in 2026?
About DKK 23 billion – 0.7% of gross national income (GNI).
Which continent receives most of Danish development aid?
Africa.
What is the relationship of the Faroe Islands and Greenland to Denmark?

They are part of the Danish Realm, have their own systems of government (home rule/self-government) and their own assemblies. Faroese and Greenlanders are Danish citizens and each elect two members to the Folketing.
Which countries border on or lie close to Denmark?
Norway (north), Sweden (north-east), Germany and Poland (south).
How big is Denmark (without Greenland and the Faroe Islands)?
A little more than 43,000 km².
What does Denmark consist of, and what is the largest island?
The Jutland peninsula and over 400 islands. Largest island: Zealand (Sjælland).
How long is Denmark's coastline?
About 7,300 km.
What is the North Sea called in Denmark, and why?
Vesterhavet (the Western Sea) – because it lies west of Denmark.
Which straits lie between Jutland and Funen, Funen and Zealand, and Zealand and Sweden?
Jutland–Funen: Lillebælt. Funen–Zealand: Storebælt. Zealand–Sweden: Øresund.
Which waters lie north of Denmark and north of Zealand and Funen?
Skagerrak (north of Denmark) and Kattegat (north of Zealand and Funen).
Which three bridge links connect the parts of the country?
The Little Belt bridges (Jutland–Funen), the Great Belt link (Funen–Zealand) and the Øresund link (Denmark–Sweden).
What is Denmark's northernmost point?
Grenen, north-east of Skagen – where Skagerrak and Kattegat meet.
What is Denmark's southernmost point?
Gedser Odde on Falster (by the Baltic Sea).
What is Denmark's westernmost point?
Blåvands Huk in West Jutland.
What is Denmark's easternmost point?
Ertholmene, east of Bornholm.
What is Denmark's highest natural point called, and how high is it?
Møllehøj in East Jutland – about 170 metres.
Where are there cliffs/rocks in Denmark?
On Bornholm (one of the few places).
How many people live in Denmark, and how many are immigrants or descendants?
About six million. About one million (17%) are immigrants or descendants.
How many live in the capital area?
About two million (about a third of the population).
What are Denmark's five largest cities (largest first)?
Copenhagen, Aarhus (approx. 300,000), Odense (approx. 200,000), Aalborg (approx. 125,000), Esbjerg (approx. 75,000).
When did the first people come to Denmark, and how did they live?
Around 12,500 BC – by hunting and fishing.
When did people start farming the land and keeping livestock?
Around 4,000 BC.
When did the first real towns appear, and which town is mentioned?
From around AD 700 – e.g. Ribe.
When was the Viking Age?
What is the Norse religion of the Viking Age called, and who was king of the gods?
Asatro (Norse paganism). The king of the gods was Odin.
Who were Freja and Thor in Norse religion?
Freja: goddess of fertility. Thor: god of thunder/war.
Who raised the Jelling Stone, and what is it called?
Harald Bluetooth (died 987). 'Denmark's baptism certificate' – it says that he united Denmark and made the Danes Christian.
When was Harald Bluetooth baptised?
Around 965.
Name Viking fortresses and towns from the Viking Age.
Fortresses: Trelleborg and Fyrkat. Towns: Odense, Aalborg and Aarhus.
Who conquered England in 1013, and who was the most important Danish king in England?
Sweyn Forkbeard (1013). Canute (Knud) the Great (reigned 1018–1035).
When did England have Danish kings?
For about 30 years up to 1042.
What happened to King Knud the Holy in 1086?
He was killed by the nobles.
Which church was the Danish church part of for the first 500–600 years?
The Roman Catholic Church.
How many churches were there in Denmark around 1250?
Up to 3,000.
Which four estates were there in the Middle Ages?
The clergy, the nobility, the burghers and the peasants.
When did the plague come to Denmark, and how many died?
Around 1350 – about a third of the population.
What was the Kalmar Union, and who was Margrete I?
A union of Denmark, Norway and Sweden from 1397 to 1523. Margrete I held power in the three kingdoms until her death in 1412.
When were Denmark and Norway in a union?
Right up until 1814.
What was the Reformation of 1536?

The Danish church broke with the Catholic Church and the Pope. Protestantism was introduced, the king became head of the church, the Bible was translated into Danish (first in 1550), and the king took over about a third of the country's farmland.
Who was Christian IV, and which buildings are known from his time?
King 1588–1648. Børsen (the Old Stock Exchange), the Round Tower (Rundetårn) and Rosenborg in Copenhagen.
Which territories did Denmark lose to Sweden in 1658?
Skåne, Halland and Blekinge.
When did Denmark become a hereditary monarchy and an absolute monarchy?
Hereditary monarchy in 1660, absolute monarchy in 1661. Before that it was an elective monarchy (the king was elected by the nobility).
When did absolute monarchy last?
What was the stavnsbånd (adscription), and when was it abolished?
It forced most peasants to work for a particular landowner and live in a particular place. Abolished in 1788 (the agricultural reforms).
What did the agricultural reforms mean for the peasants?
They could decide for themselves where to live and work, and own their own land – new independent farmers. Many farms were moved out into the fields.
What did Frederik VII do in 1848?
Gave up his absolute power and became a constitutional monarch.
When was the Constitution signed, and what did it mean?
5 June 1849. Two legislative assemblies: the Folketing and the Landsting (together: the Rigsdag).
Who could not vote under the 1849 Constitution?
Women, the poor and men under 30. That changed with the constitutional amendment of 1915.
What happened in 1864?
A war between the German Confederation and Denmark – Denmark lost the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein and became much smaller.
What was done to create growth after 1864?
The Jutland heath was cultivated, and farmers switched to breeding animals (butter, bacon, eggs) instead of only grain.
When were Venstre, Højre/the Conservatives, the Social Liberals and the Social Democrats founded?
Venstre: 1870. Højre became the Conservative People's Party in 1915–16. The Social Liberals (Det Radikale Venstre): 1905. The Social Democrats: the 1870s.
Who voted for Venstre and Højre?
Venstre: most farmers. Højre: landowners, the well-off in the towns, police, army and civil servants.
What was the significance of the railways (from the 1840s) and industrialisation (after 1870)?
Faster transport – and factories in the towns, where poor farm workers moved. The working class emerged.
Was Denmark neutral during World War I?
When was Denmark occupied during World War II?
9 April 1940, by German troops.
When did cooperation with the Germans break down?
August 1943 – the government resigned and the army was disbanded.
When was Denmark liberated?
5 May 1945 – by British troops.
1949 – Denmark gave up its policy of neutrality.
What was the Cold War?
A struggle between the superpowers the USA and the Soviet Union (NATO versus the Warsaw Pact) over military strength and ideology: liberal market economy versus communist planned economy.
What was the Marshall Plan?
From 1948 to 1951 the USA gave large sums of money to Western Europe (including Denmark) for reconstruction and to prevent the spread of communism.
When was SF founded?
1958–59 – by members who left the Communist Party of Denmark.
What did Marshall aid mean for agriculture?
Modernisation with tractors and combine harvesters. Many people moved from the countryside to the towns in the 1950s.
When was the welfare state expanded?
Especially in the 1960s and 1970s (state pension, nurseries, kindergartens, nursing homes, more education).
What is the period 1957–1973 called?
'The happy 60s' – great economic progress, high growth and work for almost everyone.
Where did foreign workers come from in the 1960s?
Most from Turkey, former Yugoslavia and Pakistan.
What was the youth rebellion?
From the end of the 1960s young people rebelled against old-fashioned norms – new family forms, living together without marriage, communes.
When was free abortion introduced, and what is the limit today?
1973 (up to the 12th week). In 2025 raised to the 18th week.
When was the contraceptive pill introduced in Denmark?
When was it forbidden to hit children at school, and when for parents?
At school: 1967. For parents: 1997.
When was the equal pay law passed?
How large a majority voted yes to EC membership in 1973?
63.4 percent.
Why did an economic crisis hit Denmark in the 1970s?
Because oil prices rose sharply in 1973 and 1979 (Denmark produced only a little oil at the time).
When did Denmark get a centre-right (borgerlig) government after a long period of Social Democrats?
1982 – it was in office for over ten years (until 1993).
What did the Folketing decide in 1985 about nuclear power?
That no nuclear power plants would be built in Denmark.
Which former prime ministers are mentioned (with their periods)?
Poul Nyrup Rasmussen (1993–2001), Anders Fogh Rasmussen (2001–09), Lars Løkke Rasmussen (2009–11 and 2015–19), Helle Thorning-Schmidt (2011–15).
When did the Danish People's Party first enter the Folketing?
1998 – after debate about immigration and integration policy.
What tightening of immigration policy was carried out?

Harder family reunification, lower social assistance for newcomers without work and stricter requirements for Danish citizenship (longer residence, work, no serious crime, language and knowledge of society).
How many years were the Social Democrats in government between 1929 and 1982?
41 years in total.
Since 1982, how many years has there been a Social Democratic and a centre-right prime minister respectively (according to the material)?
17 years with a Social Democratic prime minister and 24 years with a centre-right one.
Which economic crisis hit Denmark in 2008?
The international financial crisis – production fell 5% in 2008–09, the biggest decline since World War II.
What is a big challenge for Denmark and Europe regarding the age structure?
There are more and more elderly people compared with those of working age (15–64), because we live longer and have fewer children.
What is life expectancy in 2024–25 for women and men?
Women 83.9 years (compared with 76.6 in 1973–74). Men 80.3 years (compared with 70.8 in 1973–74).
What is the fertility rate (children per woman) in 2025 and in 1973?
Which reforms have been made to get more people into the labour market?
Higher pension age, a shorter unemployment benefit period and lower tax on earned income.
When did the coronavirus come to Denmark, and when was the first Dane vaccinated?
First case in February 2020. First vaccination in December 2020. About 90% are vaccinated.
Who is called 'the father of Danish literature', and what did he write?
Ludvig Holberg (1684–1754): the comedy 'Jeppe på Bjerget' (Jeppe of the Hill), 'Epistler' (Epistles) and the novel 'Niels Klim's Underground Travels' (1741).
Who was H.C. Andersen?
Author (1805–1875), born in Odense. World-famous for his fairy tales (translated into about 125 languages), e.g. 'The Fir Tree' and 'The Ugly Duckling'.
Who was P.S. Krøyer?
Painter (1851–1909), born in Stavanger. Painted in Skagen in the 1880s–90s, e.g. 'Hip, Hip, Hurrah!' (1888). Works at the Skagen Museum.
